claim: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a debilitating neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene.
source: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a debilitating neurodevelopmental disorder (Hagberg, 1985) caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Hagberg, 1985; Amir et al., 1999) establishing the disease and its genetic cause.

claim: All key cell types (neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes) in the brain have been shown to contribute to RTT disease etiology.
source: RTT is a complex disease, as all key cell types (neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes) in the brain have been shown to contribute to the disease etiology (Ballas et al., 2009; Chao et al., 2010; Derecki et al., 2012; Fyffe et al., 2008; Lioy et al., 2011; Luikenhuis et al., 2004; Maezawa and Jin, 2010; Maezawa et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2013; Samaco et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating contributions from different brain cell types.

claim: MeCP2 is expressed at high levels in neurons in a temporal and spatial pattern closely tracking neuronal maturation.
source: because MeCP2 is expressed at high levels in neurons in a temporal and spatial pattern closely tracking neuronal maturation (Akbarian et al., 2001; Shahbazian et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Akbarian et al., 2001; Shahbazian et al., 2002) characterizing MeCP2 expression patterns.

claim: Specific subsets of RTT-like phenotypes were observed in mouse models when Mecp2 is deleted in specific neuronal subtypes.
source: Not surprisingly, specific subsets of RTT-like phenotypes were observed in mouse models when Mecp2 is deleted in specific neuronal subtypes (Chao et al., 2010; Fyffe et al., 2008; Samaco et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior mouse model studies (Chao et al., 2010; Fyffe et al., 2008; Samaco et al., 2009).

claim: Astrocytes express MeCP2, and loss of MeCP2 in astrocytes causes neuronal defects in a non-cell autonomous manner.
source: Recently, a series of studies have reported that astrocytes express MeCP2, loss of MeCP2 in astrocytes causes neuronal defects in a non-cell autonomous manner, and restoring MeCP2 expression to normal level in astrocytes alone rescues some disease symptoms (Ballas et al., 2009; Lioy et al., 2011; Maezawa et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Ballas et al., 2009; Lioy et al., 2011; Maezawa et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2014) on astrocyte MeCP2 expression and function.

claim: Cell type specific deletion of Mecp2 in astrocytes alone is not sufficient to generate most of the RTT-like phenotypes in mice.
source: Intriguingly, cell type specific deletion of Mecp2 in astrocytes alone is not sufficient to generate most of the RTT-like phenotypes in mice (Lioy et al., 2011), suggesting the loss of function or malfunction of MeCP2 in astrocytes is not the initial cause of the disease, yet is required to maintain the disease progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study (Lioy et al., 2011) on astrocyte-specific Mecp2 deletion.

claim: More than 90% of the cells were GFAP+ in cultures used in the study.
source: On average, more than 90% of the cells were GFAP +in cultures used in our study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1, which quantify GFAP+ cells.

claim: A significantly higher percentage of mutant astrocytes (30 ± 3% in MT vs. 18 ± 2% in WT, n = 26 randomly selected fields in each genotype, p=0.001) showed spontaneous oscillation in cytosolic Ca2+ levels.
source: A significantly higher percentage of mutant astrocytes (30 ± 3% in MT vs. 18 ± 2% in WT, n = 26 randomly selected fields in each genotype, p=0.001) showed spontaneous oscillation in cytosolic Ca2+ levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 1C showing statistical comparison between mutant and wild-type astrocytes.

claim: In the soma, the mutant cells had a significantly higher frequency (0.74 ± 0.02/min in MT vs. 0.41 ± 0.01/min in WT, n = 408 cells in MT and n = 280 cells in WT, p<0.001) of spontaneous calcium oscillations than their congenic wild type controls.
source: In the soma, the mutant cells had a significantly higher frequency (0.74 ± 0.02/min in MT vs. 0.41 ± 0.01/min in WT, n = 408 cells in MT and n = 280 cells in WT, p<0.001; Figure 1C) and slightly higher amplitude (Table 2) than their congenic wild type controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 1C showing statistical comparison of calcium oscillation frequency.

claim: The R294X mutant astrocytes had significantly higher peak amplitude (4.60 ± 0.07 in MT vs. 4.04 ± 0.07 in WT, n = 567 cells in MT and n = 811 cells in WT, p<0.001) of ATP-induced Ca2+ rise than the congenic wild type control.
source: Moreover, the R294X mutant astrocytes had significantly higher peak amplitude (4.60 ± 0.07 in MT vs. 4.04 ± 0.07 in WT, n = 567 cells in MT and n = 811 cells in WT, p<0.001) of ATP-induced Ca2+ rise than the congenic wild type control (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 1D-E showing statistical comparison of ATP-induced calcium responses.

claim: The increase in ATP-induced Ca2+ rise in human RTT mutant astrocytes was unlikely to be mediated by the P2 receptors, because no difference was detected in the expression level of any P2X or P2Y receptor family members between the wild type and mutant RTT astrocytes by RNA-seq and microarray analysis.
source: The increase in ATP-induced Ca2+ rise in human RTT mutant astrocytes was unlikely to be mediated by the P2 receptors, because no difference was detected in the expression level of any P2X or P2Y receptor family members between the wild type and mutant RTT astrocytes by RNA-seq and microarray analysis (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and microarray data (not shown) indicating no change in P2 receptor expression.

claim: Similar observations of altered Ca2+ activities were made in human astrocytes carrying the rare RTT-causing V247fs mutation.
source: Similar observations of altered Ca2+ activities were made in human astrocytes carrying the rare RTT-causing V247fs mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing calcium activity in V247fs mutant astrocytes.

claim: Both spontaneous and pharmacologically evoked cytosolic Ca2+ activity appeared abnormal in mutant human RTT astrocytes differentiated from patient-specific iPSCs and grown in the absence of neurons.
source: Thus, both spontaneous and pharmacologically evoked cytosolic Ca2+ activity appeared abnormal in mutant human RTT astrocytes differentiated from patient-specific iPSCs and grown in the absence of neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing abnormal calcium activity in iPSC-derived astrocytes cultured without neurons.

claim: Expression of wild type MECP2 significantly reduced the percentage of cells with spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation (20 ± 2% in MECP2/GFP vs. 36 ± 4% in GFP, n = 6 randomly selected fields in each group, p=0.006) in mutant human RTT astrocytes.
source: When Ca2+ activity was recorded (Figure 2B), the percentage of cells with spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation was significantly reduced by the expression of wild type MECP2, compared with expression of GFP alone, in the mutant human RTT astrocytes (20 ± 2% in MECP2/GFP vs. 36 ± 4% in GFP, n = 6 randomly selected fields in each group, p=0.006; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 2C showing rescue of calcium phenotype by MECP2 expression.

claim: In the cells detected with spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation, both the frequency (0.27 ± 0.06/min in MECP2/GFP vs. 0.59 ± 0.06/min in GFP, n = 21 cells in MECP2/GFP and n = 32 cells in GFP, p<0.001) and amplitude (1.65 ± 0.08 in MECP2/GFP vs. 1.75 ± 0.03 in GFP, n = 62 events in MECP2/GFP and n = 209 events in GFP, p<0.001) were significantly reduced by the exogenous expression of wild type MECP2 as compared with expression of GFP alone.
source: In the cells detected with spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation, both the frequency (0.27 ± 0.06/min in MECP2/GFP vs. 0.59 ± 0.06/min in GFP, n = 21 cells in MECP2/GFP and n = 32 cells in GFP, p<0.001; Figure 2C) and amplitude (1.65 ± 0.08 in MECP2/GFP vs. 1.75 ± 0.03 in GFP, n = 62 events in MECP2/GFP and n = 209 events in GFP, p<0.001) were significantly reduced by the exogenous expression of wild type MECP2 as compared with expression of GFP alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 2C showing rescue of calcium oscillation frequency and amplitude by MECP2 expression.

claim: Expression of wild type MECP2 significantly reduced the elevated level of pharmacologically evoked Ca2+ response in mutant human RTT astrocytes (3.90 ± 0.13 in MECP2/GFP vs. 4.20 ± 0.10 in GFP, n = 96 cells in MECP2/GFP and n = 123 cells in GFP, p=0.022).
source: In addition, expression of wild type MECP2 significantly reduced the elevated level of pharmacologically evoked Ca2+ response in mutant human RTT astrocytes (3.90 ± 0.13 in MECP2/GFP vs. 4.20 ± 0.10 in GFP, n = 96 cells in MECP2/GFP and n = 123 cells in GFP, p=0.022; Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 2D-E showing rescue of ATP-evoked calcium response by MECP2 expression.

claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation was detected in significantly higher percentage of Mecp2 null astrocytes than in wild type controls (67 ± 5% in Mecp2-/y vs. 47 ± 6% in WT, n = 19 randomly chosen fields in both Mecp2-/y and WT, p=0.01).
source: Similar to our findings in human RTT astrocytes, spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation (Figure 3A–B) was detected in significantly higher percentage of Mecp2 null astrocytes than in wild type controls (67 ± 5% in Mecp2-/y vs. 47 ± 6% in WT, n = 19 randomly chosen fields in both Mecp2-/y and WT, p=0.01; Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 3C showing increased percentage of Mecp2 null mouse astrocytes with spontaneous calcium oscillations.

claim: In cells that showed spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation, significantly higher frequency (2.01 ± 0.04/min in Mecp2-/y vs. 1.64 ± 0.03/min in WT, n = 575 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 439 cells in WT, p<0.001) was observed in the soma of Mecp2 null astrocytes than in wild type astrocytes.
source: In cells that showed spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation, significantly higher frequency (2.01 ± 0.04/min in Mecp2-/y vs. 1.64 ± 0.03/min in WT, n = 575 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 439 cells in WT, p<0.001; Figure 3C) and slightly higher amplitude (Table 2) were observed in the soma of Mecp2 null astrocytes than in wild type astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 3C showing increased frequency of calcium oscillations in Mecp2 null mouse astrocytes.

claim: Significantly higher amplitude was detected in primary Mecp2 null mouse astrocytes (7.25 ± 0.23 in Mecp2-/y vs. 6.54 ± 0.12 in WT, n = 153 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 278 cells in WT, p=0.04) than in wild type astrocytes for pharmacologically evoked Ca2+ response.
source: As for pharmacologically evoked Ca2+ response, significantly higher amplitude was detected in primary Mecp2 null mouse astrocytes (7.25 ± 0.23 in Mecp2-/y vs. 6.54 ± 0.12 in WT, n = 153 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 278 cells in WT, p=0.04) than in wild type astrocytes (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 3D-E showing increased ATP-evoked calcium response in Mecp2 null mouse astrocytes.

claim: Higher frequency (0.59 ± 0.01/min in Mecp2-/y vs. 0.47 ± 0.01/min in WT, n = 337 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 293 cells in WT, p<0.001) of spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation was observed in the soma of SR101+ cells in Mecp2 null slices than in wild type slices.
source: Similar to our observation in cultured human patient-specific iPSC derived astrocytes and primary mouse astrocytes, higher frequency (0.59 ± 0.01/min in Mecp2-/y vs. 0.47 ± 0.01/min in WT, n = 337 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 293 cells in WT, p<0.001) and slightly higher amplitude (Table 2) of spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation was observed in the soma of SR101+ cells in Mecp2 null slices than in wild type slices (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 4B-C showing increased frequency of calcium oscillations in astrocytes in acute hippocampal slices from Mecp2 null mice.

claim: The astrocytes in Mecp2 null slices had significantly higher peak amplitude (2.75 ± 0.02 in MT vs. 2.22 ± 0.09 in WT, n = 754 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 238 cells in WT, p<0.001) of glutamate-induced Ca2+ rise than astrocytes in wild type slices.
source: In addition, the astrocytes in Mecp2 null slices had significantly higher peak amplitude (2.75 ± 0.02 in MT vs. 2.22 ± 0.09 in WT, n = 754 cells in Mecp2-/y and n = 238 cells in WT, p<0.001) of glutamate-induced Ca2+ rise than astrocytes in wild type slices (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 4D showing increased glutamate-evoked calcium response in astrocytes in acute hippocampal slices from Mecp2 null mice.

claim: Higher frequency of spontaneous oscillation of GCaMP6s fluorescence was detected in both the soma (2.15 ± 0.11/min in MT vs. 1.44 ± 0.20/min in WT, n = 57 cells in MT and n = 18 cells in WT, p=0.003) and processes (2.14 ± 0.04/min in MT vs. 1.69 ± 0.06/min in WT, n = 373 processes in MT and n = 110 processes in WT, p<0.001) of MT astrocytes in vivo.
source: When GCaMP6s fluorescence were recorded in mCherry-positive cells in the frontal cortex of 2–3 months-old live WT and floxed mice injected with AAV8-hGFAP-mCherry-Cre (MT) (Video 3–4, Figure 5A–B), higher frequency of spontaneous oscillation of GCaMP6s fluorescence was detected in both the soma (2.15 ± 0.11/min in MT vs. 1.44 ± 0.20/min in WT, n = 57 cells in MT and n = 18 cells in WT, p=0.003, Figure 5C) and processes (2.14 ± 0.04/min in MT vs. 1.69 ± 0.06/min in WT, n = 373 processes in MT and n = 110 processes in WT, p<0.001, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) of MT astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing increased frequency of calcium oscillations in astrocytes in vivo in Mecp2 null mice.

claim: The phenotype of increased frequency of spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ activity was found consistently across species, as well as in vitro, in situ, and in vivo.
source: Taken together, the phenotype of increased frequency of spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ activity was found consistently across species, as well as in vitro, in situ, and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented across multiple experimental systems (human and mouse, in vitro, in situ, and in vivo).

claim: The abnormal spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation in mutant human astrocytes persisted after Ca2+ was removed completely from extracellular environment (0 mM Ca2+ plus 2 mM EGTA).
source: Since the abnormal spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation in mutant human astrocytes persisted after Ca2+ was removed completely from extracellular environment (0 mM Ca2+ plus 2 mM EGTA, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), we measured the Ca2+ load in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the major source of intracellular Ca2+ storage.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing calcium oscillations in the absence of extracellular calcium.

claim: The amplitude of the TG-induced Ca2+ elevation was significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes than in their congenic controls (125 ± 4%. in MT vs. 100 ± 3% in WT, n = 156 cells in MT and n = 178 cells in WT, p<0.001), suggesting the mutant astrocytes had more releasable Ca2+ in the ER.
source: The amplitude of the TG-induced Ca2+ elevation was significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes than in their congenic controls (125 ± 4%. in MT vs. 100 ± 3% in WT, n = 156 cells in MT and n = 178 cells in WT, p<0.001, Figure 6A), suggesting the mutant astrocytes had more releasable Ca2+ in the ER.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 6A showing increased ER calcium load in mutant astrocytes, with an inference about the meaning of this result.

claim: When the kinetics of this Ca2+ rise was analyzed, the leakage of Ca2+ from the ER in the mutant astrocytes was much faster (time constant 54 ± 1 s in MT vs. 59 ± 1 s in WT, n = 156 cells in MT and n = 178 cells in WT, p<0.001).
source: Moreover, when the kinetics of this Ca2+ rise was analyzed, the leakage of Ca2+ from the ER in the mutant astrocytes was much faster (time constant 54 ± 1 s in MT vs. 59 ± 1 s in WT, n = 156 cells in MT and n = 178 cells in WT, p<0.001, Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 6B-C showing faster calcium leak from the ER in mutant astrocytes.

claim: Significantly higher level of Rhod-2 fluorescence was detected in the Mecp2 null cells (154 ± 7% in GFP- vs. 100 ± 5% in GFP+, n = 30 in each group, p<0.0001), indicating elevated baseline cytosolic Ca2+ level.
source: When the red-colored calcium-sensitive dye Rhod-2 was used to image baseline cytosolic Ca2+ level in the Mecp2 null (GFP-) and wild type (GFP+) astrocytes in the same culture (Figure 6D), significantly higher level of Rhod-2 fluorescence was detected in the Mecp2 null cells (154 ± 7% in GFP- vs. 100 ± 5% in GFP+, n = 30 in each group, p<0.0001; Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 6E showing elevated baseline cytosolic calcium in Mecp2 null astrocytes.

claim: No significant difference was detected in baseline cytosolic Ca2+ level between the GFP+ and GFP- cells from Mecp2+/+ female mice (107 ± 8% in GFP- vs. 100 ± 6% in GFP+, n = 31 in GFP- and n = 32 in GFP+, p=0.46).
source: As a control, astrocyte cultures were also prepared from Mecp2+/+ female mice that carry the same X chromosome-linked GFP transgene. No significant deference was detected in baseline cytosolic Ca2+ level between the GFP+ and GFP- cells (107 ± 8% in GFP- vs. 100 ± 6% in GFP+, n = 31 in GFP- and n = 32 in GFP+, p=0.46; Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 6F showing no difference in baseline cytosolic calcium in control astrocytes.

claim: Ca2+ overload in the ER, the faster Ca2+ leak rate, and the elevated baseline cytosolic Ca2+ level are significant contributors to the abnormal spontaneous and pharmacologically evoked cytosolic Ca2+ activities in the mutant RTT astrocytes.
source: These results reveal Ca2+ overload in the ER, the faster Ca2+ leak rate, and the elevated baseline cytosolic Ca2+ level as significant contributors to the abnormal spontaneous and pharmacologically evoked cytosolic Ca2+ activities in the mutant RTT astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing ER calcium overload, faster leak, and elevated baseline cytosolic calcium in mutant astrocytes.

claim: The amplitude of Ca2+ influx was significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes (2.93 ± 0.07 in MT vs. 2.41 ± 0.06 in WT, n = 156 cells in MT and n = 178 cells in WT, p<0.001), suggesting an abnormal increase of SOCE in the mutant cells.
source: Comparing to that in the congenic control, the amplitude of Ca2+ influx was significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes (2.93 ± 0.07 in MT vs. 2.41 ± 0.06 in WT, n = 156 cells in MT and n = 178 cells in WT, p<0.001; Figure 6G), suggesting an abnormal increase of SOCE in the mutant cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 6G showing increased SOCE in mutant astrocytes, with an inference about the meaning of this result.

claim: The expression of TRPC4 was found to be significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes (~27 fold increase by RNA-seq,~14 fold increase by microarray).
source: Highly relevant to the observed SOCE phenotype, the expression of the transient receptor potential cation channel, subfamily C, member 4 (TRPC4), which has been previously shown to regulate SOCE in lung vascular endothelial cells (Tiruppathi et al., 2002), was found to be significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes (~27 fold increase by RNA-seq,~14 fold increase by microarray).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and microarray data showing increased TRPC4 expression in mutant astrocytes, and a citation to prior work (Tiruppathi et al., 2002) linking TRPC4 to SOCE.

claim: Western blot analysis using protein lysates from mutant human RTT astrocytes and their congenic controls confirmed the increased expression of TRPC4.
source: Western blot analysis using protein lysates from mutant human RTT astrocytes and their congenic controls also confirmed the increased expression of TRPC4 (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 6H-I showing increased TRPC4 protein in mutant astrocytes.

claim: Immunostaining with TrpC4 antibody detected significantly higher immunoreactivity in GFAP positive astrocytes in hippocampal sections from the Mecp2 null mouse brains as compared with that in wild type mouse brains.
source: Immunostaining with TrpC4 antibody also detected significantly higher immunoreactivity in GFAP positive astrocytes in hippocampal sections from the Mecp2 null mouse brains as compared with that in wild type mouse brains (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing increased TRPC4 immunoreactivity in Mecp2 null mouse astrocytes.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis revealed significant MeCP2 occupancy at the promoter of Trpc4, suggesting direct regulation of Trpc4 transcription by MeCP2.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis revealed significant MeCP2 occupancy at the promoter of Trpc4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting direct regulation of Trpc4 transcription by MeCP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 showing MeCP2 binding to the Trpc4 promoter, with an inference about the meaning of this result.

claim: Significantly higher density of ML204 sensitive inward current (at −70 mV) was detected in the R294X mutant human RTT astrocytes (−0.93 ± 0.01 pA/pF in MT vs. −0.62 ± 0.08 pA/pF in WT, n = 14 cells in MT and n = 15 cells in WT, p=0.01).
source: Significantly higher density of ML204 sensitive inward current (at −70 mV) was detected in the R294X mutant human RTT astrocytes (−0.93 ± 0.01 pA/pF in MT vs. −0.62 ± 0.08 pA/pF in WT, n = 14 cells in MT and n = 15 cells in WT, p=0.01; Figure 6J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in the text and Figure 6J-K showing increased ML204-sensitive current in mutant astrocytes.

claim: The ML204-sensitive current was significantly reduced when mutant human RTT astrocytes were infected with a lentivirus expressing an shRNA specific against TRPC4 (−0.61 ± 0.10 pA/pF in MT infected with lenti-GFP-shTRPC4 vs. −1.04 ± 0.05 pA/pF in MT infected with lenti-GFP, n = 9 cells in each condition, p=0.006), suggesting the current is dependent on TRPC4.
source: Moreover, this current was significantly reduced when mutant human RTT astrocytes were infected with a lentivirus expressing an shRNA specific against TRPC4 (−0.61 ± 0.10 pA/pF in MT infected with lenti-GFP-shTRPC4 vs. −1.04 ± 0.05 pA/pF in MT infected with lenti-GFP, n = 9 cells in each condition, p=0.006, Figure 6L–M), suggesting the current is dependent on TRPC4.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in the text and Figure 6L-M showing reduction of current by TRPC4 knockdown, with an inference about the meaning of this result.

claim: The phenotypes of increased Ca2+ overload in the ER, faster Ca2+ leak from the ER, increased SOCE, and increased level of TrpC4 were also observed in primary astrocytes isolated from Mecp2 null mice.
source: Finally, the phenotypes of increased Ca2+ overload in the ER, faster Ca2+ leak from the ER, increased SOCE, and increased level of TrpC4 were also observed in primary astrocytes isolated from Mecp2 null mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 showing similar calcium and TRPC4 phenotypes in mouse astrocytes.

claim: ML204-treated Mecp2 null astrocytes showed significantly reduced amplitude of SOCE mediated Ca2+ elevation (3.15 ± 0.12 in ML204-treated group vs. 6.61 ± 0.86 in untreated, n = 18 in ML204-treated and n = 16 in untreated, p=0.0002) and lower ER Ca2+ load (1.86 ± 0.06 in ML204-treated vs. 2.47 ± 0.24 in untreated, n = 14 in ML204-treated and n = 15 in untreated, p=0.02).
source: Comparing to untreated Mecp2 null astrocytes, ML204-treated cells showed significantly reduced amplitude of SOCE mediated Ca2+ elevation (3.15 ± 0.12 in ML204-treated group vs. 6.61 ± 0.86 in untreated, n = 18 in ML204-treated and n = 16 in untreated, p=0.0002; Figure 7A) and lower ER Ca2+ load (1.86 ± 0.06 in ML204-treated vs. 2.47 ± 0.24 in untreated, n = 14 in ML204-treated and n = 15 in untreated, p=0.02; Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 7A-B showing rescue of SOCE and ER calcium phenotypes by ML204 treatment.

claim: ML204 treatment significantly reduced the percentage of Mecp2 null astrocytes showing spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation (23 ± 3% in ML204-treated vs. 46 ± 7% in untreated, n = 9 randomly chosen fields in ML204-treated and n = 8 randomly chosen fields in untreated, p=0.03) and the frequency (0.20 ± 0.01/min in ML204-treated vs. 0.31 ± 0.01/min in untreated, n = 91 cells in ML204-treated and n = 203 cells in untreated, p<0.001) and amplitude (1.64 ± 0.02 in ML204-treated vs. 1.97 ± 0.02 in untreated, n = 168 events in ML204-treated and n = 597 events in untreated, p<0.001) of such oscillations.
source: More importantly, ML204 treatment significantly reduced the percentage of Mecp2 null astrocytes showing spontaneous cytosolic Ca2+ oscillation (23 ± 3% in ML204-treated vs. 46 ± 7% in untreated, n = 9 randomly chosen fields in ML204-treated and n = 8 randomly chosen fields in untreated, p=0.03; Figure 7C) and the frequency (0.20 ± 0.01/min in ML204-treated vs. 0.31 ± 0.01/min in untreated, n = 91 cells in ML204-treated and n = 203 cells in untreated, p<0.001; Figure 7C) and amplitude (1.64 ± 0.02 in ML204-treated vs. 1.97 ± 0.02 in untreated, n = 168 events in ML204-treated and n = 597 events in untreated, p<0.001; Figure 7C) of such oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 7C showing rescue of spontaneous calcium oscillation phenotypes by ML204 treatment.

claim: Mutant astrocytes infected with lentivirus expressing shTRPC4 showed significantly reduced SOCE-mediated Ca2+ elevations (1.72 ± 0.05 in MT/Lenti-ShTRPC4-GFP vs. 2.02 ± 0.04 in MT/Lenti-GFP, n = 23 in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4 and n = 26 in MT/Lenti-GFP, p<0.0001), lower ER Ca2+ load (2.37 ± 0.16 in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4-GFP vs. 2.95 ± 0.29 in MT/Lenti-GFP, n = 23 in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4 and n = 26 in MT/Lenti-GFP, p=0.04), and lower frequency (0.42 ± 0.03/min in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4-GFP vs. 0.63 ± 0.03 in MT/Lenti-GFP, n = 86 cells in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4 and n = 79 cells in MT/Lenti-GFP, p<0.001) of the spontaneous Ca2+ elevations.
source: Comparing to those infected with lentivirus expressing GFP alone, the mutant astrocytes infected with lentivirus expressing shTRPC4 showed significantly reduced SOCE-mediated Ca2+ elevations (1.72 ± 0.05 in MT/Lenti-ShTRPC4-GFP vs. 2.02 ± 0.04 in MT/Lenti-GFP, n = 23 in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4 and n = 26 in MT/Lenti-GFP, p<0.0001; Figure 7F), lower ER Ca2+ load (2.37 ± 0.16 in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4-GFP vs. 2.95 ± 0.29 in MT/Lenti-GFP, n = 23 in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4 and n = 26 in MT/Lenti-GFP, p=0.04; Figure 7G), and lower frequency (0.42 ± 0.03/min in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4-GFP vs. 0.63 ± 0.03 in MT/Lenti-GFP, n = 86 cells in MT/Lenti-shTRPC4 and n = 79 cells in MT/Lenti-GFP, p<0.001, Figure 7H) of the spontaneous Ca2+ elevations.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 7F-H showing rescue of calcium phenotypes by TRPC4 knockdown.

claim: The pharmacological and molecular manipulations demonstrated that elevated TRPC4 expression is required for the abnormal calcium homeostasis in MeCP2 deficient astrocytes.
source: Together, the pharmacological and molecular manipulations demonstrated that elevated TRPC4 expression is required for the abnormal calcium homeostasis in MeCP2 deficient astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing rescue of calcium phenotypes by TRPC4 inhibition and knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of TRPC4 in wild type human astrocytes caused increased SOCE-mediated Ca2+ elevations (2.76. ± 0.15 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 2.36 ± 0.08 in WT/GFP, n = 52 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 55 in WT/GFP, p=0.02), higher ER Ca2+ load (3.65 ± 0.23 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 2.62 ± 0.13 in WT/GFP, n = 52 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 55 in WT/GFP, p=0.0001), more cells showing spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation (29 ± 5% in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 16 ± 3% in WT/GFP, n = 13 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 12 in WT/GFP, p=0.03), higher frequency (0.71 ± 0.04/min in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 0.45 ± 0.01/min in WT/GFP, n = 74 cells in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 100 cells in WT/GFP, p<0.001) and amplitude (1.49 ± 0.04 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 1.22 ± 0.01 in WT/GFP, n = 523 events in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 445 events in WT/GFP, p<0.001) of spontaneous Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Finally, we overexpressed TRPC4 in wild type human astrocytes (Figure 7I), and observed increased SOCE-mediated Ca2+ elevations (2.76. ± 0.15 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 2.36 ± 0.08 in WT/GFP, n = 52 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 55 in WT/GFP, p=0.02; Figure 7J), higher ER Ca2+ load (3.65 ± 0.23 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 2.62 ± 0.13 in WT/GFP, n = 52 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 55 in WT/GFP, p=0.0001; Figure 7K), more cells showing spontaneous Ca2+ oscillation (29 ± 5% in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 16 ± 3% in WT/GFP, n = 13 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 12 in WT/GFP, p=0.03; Figure 7L), higher frequency (0.71 ± 0.04/min in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 0.45 ± 0.01/min in WT/GFP, n = 74 cells in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 100 cells in WT/GFP, p<0.001; Figure 7L) and amplitude (1.49 ± 0.04 in WT/GFP-TRPC4 vs. 1.22 ± 0.01 in WT/GFP, n = 523 events in WT/GFP-TRPC4 and n = 445 events in WT/GFP, p<0.001; Figure 7L) of spontaneous Ca2+ oscillations in those cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 7I-L showing induction of calcium phenotypes by TRPC4 overexpression.

claim: Elevated TRPC4 expression is sufficient to cause abnormal calcium homeostasis in wild type astrocytes.
source: These results strongly suggest that elevated TRPC4 expression is sufficient to cause abnormal calcium homeostasis in wild type astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing induction of calcium phenotypes by TRPC4 overexpression in wild type astrocytes.

claim: Ca2+ oscillation in astrocytes could lead to activation of eNMDARs.
source: Previous work has shown that Ca2+ oscillation in astrocytes could lead to activation of eNMDARs (Fellin et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Fellin et al., 2004) linking astrocytic calcium oscillations to eNMDAR activation.

claim: A significantly higher frequency of slow inward current (SIC) was detected in acute hippocampal slices prepared from 2 to 3 weeks old Mecp2 null mice than those from the wild type littermate control (3.88 ± 0.46/20 min in Mecp2 null vs. 1.50 ± 0.39/20 min in WT, n = 16 in Mecp2 null and n = 12 in WT, p=0.001).
source: We measured activation of eNMDAR on mouse hippocampal pyramidal neurons by whole cell patch clamp recording, and detected a significantly higher frequency of a slow inward current (SIC, Figure 8A, left) in acute hippocampal slices prepared from 2 to 3 weeks old Mecp2 null mice than those from the wild type littermate control (3.88 ± 0.46/20 min in Mecp2 null vs. 1.50 ± 0.39/20 min in WT, n = 16 in Mecp2 null and n = 12 in WT, p=0.001; Figure 8A, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data presented in the text and Figure 8A showing increased SIC frequency in Mecp2 null mice.

claim: The SICs were sensitive to both D-APV (selective NMDA receptor antagonist, 50 µM) and ifenprodil (selective NR2B-containing NMDA receptor antagonist, 10 µM), suggesting they were mediated by NR2B-containing eNMDARs.
source: The SICs were sensitive to both D-APV (selective NMDA receptor antagonist, 50 µM, Figure 8B, left) and ifenprodil (selective NR2B-containing NMDA receptor antagonist, 10 µM, Figure 8B, right), suggesting they were mediated by NR2B-containing eNMDARs.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacology data presented in Figure 8B showing sensitivity of SICs to NMDAR antagonists, with an inference about the receptor subtype.

claim: Intracellular infusion of membrane-impermeable BAPTA into a single astrocyte revealed a significant reduction in the frequency of SIC (2.08 ± 0.51/20 min in Mecp2 null with BAPTA infusion into a single astrocyte vs. 5.33 ± 1.04/20 min in Mecp2 null with no treatment, n = 12 in each group, p=0.01), suggesting that the abnormally high calcium activity in astrocytes is required for the excessive activation of eNMDARs on neighboring neurons.
source: Whole cell patch clamp recording on hippocampal pyramidal neurons within the field of these dye-labeled astrocytes (i.e. with the intracellular chelator BAPTA) revealed a significant reduction in the frequency of SIC (2.08 ± 0.51/20 min in Mecp2 null with BAPTA infusion into a single astrocyte vs. 5.33 ± 1.04/20 min in Mecp2 null with no treatment, n = 12 in each group, p=0.01; Figure 8C), suggesting that the abnormally high calcium activity in astrocytes is required for the excessive activation of eNMDARs on neighboring neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data presented in the text and Figure 8C showing reduction of SIC frequency by BAPTA infusion into astrocytes, with an inference about the meaning of this result.

claim: Abnormal spontaneous calcium activity in astrocytes and excessive activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors in neighboring neurons were only observed in predominantly astrocyte-specific, but not in predominantly neuron-specific, Mecp2 knockout hippocampal slices.
source: Abnormal spontaneous calcium activity in astrocytes (Figure 8E, n = 34 in AAV-mCherry group, n = 36 in AAV-Syn-mCherry-Cre group, and n = 47 in AAV-hGFAP-mCherry-Cre group; ANOVA: F = 14.11, p<0.0001) and excessive activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors in neighboring neurons (Figure 8F, n = 38 in AAV-mCherry group, n = 21 in AAV-Syn-mCherry-Cre group, and n = 30 in AAV-hGFAP-mCherry-Cre group; ANOVA: F = 4.23, p<0.018) were only observed in predominantly astrocyte-specific, but not in predominantly neuron-specific, Mecp2 knockout hippocampal slices.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 8E-F showing calcium and SIC phenotypes only in astrocyte-specific Mecp2 knockout mice.

claim: The abnormal calcium activities in astrocytes are caused by the loss of MeCP2 function in astrocytes, and can lead to excessive activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors on neighboring neurons (even when these neighboring neurons are wild type).
source: Results from this series of genetic manipulations strongly suggest that the abnormal calcium activities in astrocytes are caused by the loss of MeCP2 function in astrocytes, and can lead to excessive activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors on neighboring neurons (even when these neighboring neurons are wild type).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented from cell-type-specific Mecp2 knockout experiments.

claim: Increased astrocytic Ca2+ activity may lead to a hyperexcitable network.
source: Beyond eNMDAR activation, several previous studies have suggested that increased astrocytic Ca2+ activity may lead to a hyperexcitable network (Gómez-Gonzalo et al., 2010; Kuchibhotla et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2005; Wetherington et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Gómez-Gonzalo et al., 2010; Kuchibhotla et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2005; Wetherington et al., 2008) linking astrocytic calcium activity to network hyperexcitability.

claim: 80–90% of RTT patients have seizures.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior clinical study (Jian et al., 2007) reporting seizure prevalence in RTT patients.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior mouse model study (D'Cruz et al., 2010) reporting spontaneous seizures in RTT mice.

claim: Epileptiform activity in Mecp2-/y neurons had shorter latency (4.5 ± 0.4 min in Mecp2-/y vs. 6.5 ± 0.6 min in wild type), higher frequency (5.6 ± 0.4 Hz in Mecp2-/y vs. 3.5 ± 0.5 Hz in wild type), longer duration (755 ± 30 ms in Mecp2-/y vs. 621 ± 39 ms in wild type), and higher amplitude (364 ± 15 pA in Mecp2-/y vs. 279 ± 28 pA in wild type) compared to wild type.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data presented in the text and Figure 8H showing increased epileptiform activity in Mecp2 null mice.

claim: Intracellular infusion of membrane impermeable BAPTA into a single astrocyte significantly reduced epileptiform activity in neighboring neurons (latency: 4.5 ± 0.4 min in Mecp2-/y vs. 5.7 ± 0.4 min in Mecp2-/y with BAPTA infusion; frequency: 5.6 ± 0.4 Hz in Mecp2-/y vs. 3.8 ± 0.5 Hz in Mecp2-/y with BAPTA infusion; duration: 755 ± 30 ms in Mecp2-/y vs. 633 ± 31 ms in Mecp2-/y with BAPTA infusion).

Figure 8H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data presented in the text and Figure 8H showing reduction of epileptiform activity by BAPTA infusion into astrocytes.

claim: These data reveal a potential link between increased astrocytic Ca2+ activity and increased network excitability.
source: Together, these data reveal a potential link between increased astrocytic Ca2+ activity and increased network excitability.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing reduction of epileptiform activity by BAPTA infusion into astrocytes.

claim: Since such increased network excitability may underlie seizure-a specific RTT symptom, these data further highlight the functional significance of abnormal Ca2+ activity in RTT.
source: Since such increased network excitability may underlie seizure-a specific RTT symptom, these data further highlight the functional significance of abnormal Ca2+ activity in RTT.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the potential clinical relevance of the network excitability findings.

claim: Abnormal calcium homeostasis is a key cell-autonomous phenotype in RTT astrocytes.
source: Our findings provide evidence that abnormal calcium homeostasis is a key cell-autonomous phenotype in RTT astrocytes, and reveal its mechanism and consequence.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented throughout the manuscript showing abnormal calcium activity in RTT astrocytes across multiple experimental systems.

claim: Abnormal calcium homeostasis in RTT astrocytes is mediated by calcium overload in the endoplasmic reticulum caused by abnormal store operated calcium entry, which is in part dependent on elevated expression of TRPC4.
source: Such abnormal calcium activity is mediated by calcium overload in the endoplasmic reticulum caused by abnormal store operated calcium entry, which is in part dependent on elevated expression of TRPC4.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing ER calcium overload, increased SOCE, elevated TRPC4 expression, and rescue of calcium phenotypes by TRPC4 inhibition/knockdown.

claim: The abnormal calcium activity in RTT astrocytes leads to excessive activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors (eNMDARs) on neighboring neurons and increased network excitability in Mecp2 knockout mice.
source: Furthermore, the abnormal calcium activity leads to excessive activation of extrasynaptic NMDA receptors (eNMDARs) on neighboring neurons and increased network excitability in Mecp2 knockout mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented showing increased SIC frequency and epileptiform activity in Mecp2 null mice, and rescue of these phenotypes by BAPTA infusion into astrocytes.

claim: Both the abnormal astrocytic calcium activity and the excessive activation of eNMDARs are caused by Mecp2 deletion in astrocytes in vivo.
source: Finally, both the abnormal astrocytic calcium activity and the excessive activation of eNMDARs are caused by Mecp2 deletion in astrocytes in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data presented from cell-type-specific Mecp2 knockout experiments showing calcium and SIC phenotypes only in astrocyte-specific knockout mice.

claim: TRPC4 has been previously shown to regulate SOCE in lung vascular endothelial cells.
source: Highly relevant to the observed SOCE phenotype, the expression of the transient receptor potential cation channel, subfamily C, member 4 (TRPC4), which has been previously shown to regulate SOCE in lung vascular endothelial cells (Tiruppathi et al., 2002), was found to be significantly higher in the mutant human RTT astrocytes (~27 fold increase by RNA-seq,~14 fold increase by microarray).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Tiruppathi et al., 2002) showing TRPC4 regulation of SOCE in endothelial cells.

claim: No major cell autonomous phenotype in astrocytes has been characterized in depth in RTT prior to this study.
source: Although a few studies have reported gene expression changes in Mecp2 mutant mouse astrocytes (Forbes-Lorman et al., 2014; Yasui et al., 2013), no major cell autonomous phenotype in astrocytes has been characterized in depth.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the prior literature, with citations to prior studies (Forbes-Lorman et al., 2014; Yasui et al., 2013) that reported gene expression changes but not major cell autonomous phenotypes.

claim: Identification of cell autonomous phenotypes in astrocytes is essential for understanding astrocyte dysfunction in RTT and will help determine the mechanism underlying its non-cell autonomous effects on neurons.
source: Thus, identification of cell autonomous phenotypes in astrocytes not only is essential for our understanding of astrocyte dysfunction in RTT, but also will help us to determine the mechanism underlying its non-cell autonomous effects on neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the importance of identifying cell autonomous phenotypes in astrocytes for understanding RTT pathogenesis.

claim: The difference between wild type and mutant iPSC lines generated from the same RTT patients is the entire X chromosome, making 'congenic' a more accurate term than 'isogenic' to define these lines.
source: We have used the term 'isogenic' to describe these RTT iPSC lines in our previous reports (Ananiev et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2014). However, given that the difference between wild type and mutant iPSC lines generated from the same RTT patients is the entire X chromosome, congenic is a more accurate term to define these lines.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the genetic difference between the iPSC lines, with citations to prior reports (Ananiev et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2014) that used the term 'isogenic'.

claim: Ionophore A23187 was used as a loading control for calcium imaging experiments.
source: Ionophore A23187 was used as a loading control (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing A23187-induced calcium elevations.

claim: The exogenous expression of MECP2 in mutant astrocytes infected with lenti-MECP2/GFP was not significant above the endogenous level in wild type astrocytes.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing similar MeCP2 levels in rescued mutant and wild type astrocytes, with an inference about the meaning of this result.

evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing loss of MeCP2 in GCaMP6s-positive cells after AAV-mediated Cre expression.

claim: GCaMP6s positive cells from WT mice were MeCP2 positive.

evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing MeCP2 expression in GCaMP6s-positive cells from wild type mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by data (not shown) indicating no change in expression of other TRP channels in mutant astrocytes.

source: Furthermore, it is worth noting that abnormal calcium activities in astrocytes have been implicated in other neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease(Kuchibhotla et al., 2009), suggesting abnormal calcium homeostasis in astrocytes may be a common pathological event in neurological diseases.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Lu et al., 2016) reporting increased neuronal synchrony in Mecp2 mutant mice.

claim: It remains debatable whether excessive activation of eNMDARs leads to increased neuronal synchrony and seizure in general.
source: Although it remains debatable whether excessive activation of eNMDARs leads to increased neuronal synchrony and seizure in general (Angulo et al., 2004; Fellin et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2005), increased synchronous neuronal firing has recently been observed in the hippocampus of both male Mecp2-/y and female Mecp2+/- mice(Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the literature, with citations to prior studies (Angulo et al., 2004; Fellin et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2005) showing conflicting results on the relationship between eNMDAR activation and neuronal synchrony/seizure.

claim: 100% of mCherry-positive cells were positive for GFAP in sections from Mecp2flox/y male mice injected with AAV8-hGFAP-mCherry-Cre.
source: Immunohistological analysis of sections from Mecp2flox/y male mice injected with AAV8-hGFAP-mCherry-Cre showed that 100% of mCherry-positive cells were positive for GFAP (right, Figure 8D, Table 3) and negative for MeCP2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), and that ~ 27% of GFAP-positive cells were positive for mCherry (Table 3), suggesting successful deletion of Mecp2 in about one third of the astrocytes in the forebrain.

source: Immunohistological analysis of sections from Mecp2flox/y male mice injected with AAV8-hGFAP-mCherry-Cre showed that 100% of mCherry-positive cells were positive for GFAP (right, Figure 8D, Table 3) and negative for MeCP2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), and that ~ 27% of GFAP-positive cells were positive for mCherry (Table 3), suggesting successful deletion of Mecp2 in about one third of the astrocytes in the forebrain.
